This will lead to reductions in energy use, cost savings, and fewer challenges in obtaining new technologies for identified stakeholder groups. 11 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. 2.4.1.2 Background Energy efficiency in the building industry is not new. The first Energy Policy and Conservation Act was signed into law by President Gerald Ford in 1975. So why don’t we see the latest and greatest building technologies everywhere? For example, light-emitting diode (LED) lightbulbs have been on the market for nearly two decades at lower and lower costs, yet only 54% of high-income households and 39% of low- income households report having LED bulbs installed (U.S. Energy Information Administration 2022). Similarly, wireless IoT sensors and devices are improving how we interact with and control devices in our homes and our workplaces. Many of these systems require broadband internet, but only 57% of low-income households in the United States have broadband internet (Pew Research Center 2021). In addition, there is an almost 10% difference in access to broadband internet for rural communities compared to urban and suburban communities. An estimated 39% of people living in rural areas lack access to the basic fixed broadband service needed for many of these technologies to function (Levin and Mattey 2017). Heat pump water heaters (HPWHs) are another example of a newer technology that can save a substantial portion of energy for domestic hot water building loads—particularly for residential and multifamily dwellings. An apartment building with multiple generations of families who are often home will have an elevated hot water usage profile compared to an apartment building with single-family tenants who are mostly away during the day. HPWHs subjected to higher usage profiles will require the use of a backup electric coil more often, leading to less efficient operation and potentially higher utility costs. Adding to the complexity of the situation, tenants renting an apartment are often responsible for utility bills but do not typically own their water heaters or have a say in the type of equipment purchased by the landlord or owners. This seemingly energy-efficient technology investment might actually increase the utility bill for certain tenant behaviors. The decision to incorporate HPWHs should consider performance, usage, and costs. The initial cost of a new technology is an important factor for deployment, and solutions to reduce this cost are needed to help increase market adoption and impact. However, this approach may overlook subtleties specific to subsets of the population where reducing cost may not be enough to achieve market adoption potential. For example, there could be perception or lack of awareness barriers, or barriers specific to certain stakeholder groups that cannot be seen through a cost-only lens (Cort 2013).
